chapter: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
title: Joining ASCAP and publishing through Robbins
summary: Before 1945 McRae's songs sat with Robbins Music; joining ASCAP with a whole catalog let him collect back revenue.

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Royalties, publishing and who owns the song

blocks.x: You say you joined ASCAP in '45.
In 1945, yeah.
'45, okay.
Up until the time that you did join ASCAP, and you were composing early songs like Traffic Jam and so on, what did you do with them?
I mean, how did they get into ASCAP?
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
Well, we didn't -- The publishers had them.
I see. you didn't (Inaudible) exactly publish them --

All our things were in Robbins Music, you know. See, when I was writing for Artie, Artie was a arranger and he had signed with Robbins Music for all his music -- it went into Robbins. Everything like -- Way before I joined Artie -- remember the little band he had? You know, he was writing -- he put all his music with Jack Robbins that time. Meanwhile, I became affiliated with Jack Robbins through -- from the Savoy with Chick, you know. And all the time that we were writing, I just put my things in the publishing company. I didn't bother about joining ASCAP. Because you remember, that I didn't know too much about ASCAP at that time. Another thing, we were travelling a lot. We stayed on the road with Chick. Didn't
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943

give you too much chance to fool around to much with music. I think in '45, when I joined Louie, I become aware of all the revenues that you could get from ASCAP. You must remember, ASCAP was still growing, growing and growing. I think when I joined ASCAP, they was getting like eight million or nine million dollars a year (inaudible). Now it's about triple that, you know. In the 40's (inaudible). So, I didn't lose too much because eventually I got my revenue -- the things that were in Robbins -- Robbins was paying me royalties, you know.
I see. So it really didn't matter so much --
Well, it did matter --
-- at the time.
-- because I finally got -- When I did join ASCAP, I got a lot of royalties -- revenue that was still there that I could

still collect from, you know. Because when I went into ASCAP, I went in with a whole big catalog. I didn't go in with just one or two songs.
In other words, they held it for you, or they --
Well it was still there. I could still pick it up.
You could get it, and then when you brought your catalog in, they saw the songs that had been registered with --
Yeah, registered there. I could still pick up some of my revenue.
Who was the music publishing company, or, what was it that you had 'Traffic Jam'?
Robbins Music.
Oh.
The big three. We call it the big three, Robbins Music. Remember I was telling you that Jack Robbins was the one that give me the idea on Ella, you

know, about the -- because Jack was a -- he also run -- Robbins Music was owned by Warner Brothers. I finally found out that. And all these picture tunes were coming out of California that time. It was a lot of big pictures coming out. And we would get a shot at all these tunes --
